SOURCE DETAIL FOR SELF-STUDY
WELCOME
2
WELCOME
Ask, or delegate — prompting does both
Prompting is the one AI skill that transfers everywhere: every assistant, every vendor, every year. Models change monthly; the craft compounds.
The same skill has two modes. Generative: you ask, it writes, you act. Agentic: you brief it, it plans, uses tools, checks itself, and delivers.
Each mode needs a different kind of prompt — that distinction is the backbone of this training.
The 10-second version: 
a generative prompt describes what to write.
An agentic prompt describes a job to run — Part 5 teaches that mode properly.
PROMPT 1/7
Two modes, felt — opens your course log
STEP 1 · TYPE THIS → “This chat is my course log for a prompting course. Remember every prompt I run — at the end I’ll ask for a report.”
WHY → the log becomes the final exercise.
STEP 2 · TYPE THIS → “First job: write a farewell card for a coworker.”
WHY → generative mode — instant, guessing every unknown.
STEP 3 · TYPE THIS → “Now don’t write it — interview me first, then wait.”
WHY → delegate mode’s seed — the questions come to YOU.
✂ copy-paste, don’t retype: tab EX1-TwoModes of your Course Workbook

BLOCK 1 · FOUNDATIONS
1 · The primer — how this actually works
2 · Models & tools — the landscape
BLOCK 2 · THE CRAFT
3 · Prompt engineering — anatomy + techniques
4 · The playbook — worked examples & demos
BLOCK 3 · DELEGATION

6 · Prompts as assets · wrap-up
You leave with:
•  Course Workbook — every exercise, copy-paste ready
•  13-template prompt library + Template Creator
•  Taxonomy reference + one-page cheat sheet
•  Field Guide — the elements + the works/myth/expired compendium
•  Team conventions for storing & versioning prompts

SOURCE DETAIL FOR SELF-STUDY
PART 1 · A SHORT HISTORY
4
SEVENTY YEARS IN ONE SLIDE
Four eras: rules → learning → generative → agentic
Rules
1950s–1990s · symbolic AI, expert systems
if…?
then A
else B
Humans hand-code the logic: “if X then Y.” Rules shine, then crack on messy reality. Hype outruns results twice: the “AI winters.”
Gave us: expert systems doing real work — MYCIN diagnosing infections, XCON configuring computers.
Learning
1990s–2010s · machine learning, neural networks
Stop writing rules — let the system find patterns in examples. 2012: deep nets + GPUs crush image recognition (AlexNet: 15.3% error vs 26.2%).
Gave us: spam filters, search ranking, recommendations, image recognition.
Generative
2017– · transformers, LLMs
The
audit
is
…?
The Transformer (2017) lets models train on the whole internet. Predict-the-next-word at that scale writes, summarizes, codes.
Gave us: ChatGPT (2022), image generators — AI everyone can talk to.
Agentic
2024– · reasoning models, tool use
PLAN
ACT
CHECK
Models get “arms”: tools, browsers, files, code. Reasoning models plan multi-step work; agents execute with limited supervision.
Giving us: coding agents, office agents, deep-research modes — AI you delegate to.
Why the last decade exploded — scaling laws (2020): bigger model + more data + more compute = predictably better results. Progress stopped being a research gamble and became an investment roadmap.

3) Pause once on “AI winters”: over-promising collapsed funding twice — skepticism is historically earned.
4) Close on the amber band: scaling laws.

SOURCE DETAIL FOR SELF-STUDY
PART 1 · A SHORT HISTORY
5
THE DECADE THAT CHANGED WORK
Each leap has a name — 2017 → 2026
2017
The Transformer — “Attention Is All You Need” (Google) — the architecture behind every model since
2020
Scaling laws + few-shot — GPT-3: show examples in the prompt, it does the task — prompt engineering is born
2022
Instruction tuning + RLHF — human feedback turns a predictor into an assistant; ChatGPT hits 100M users in 2 months
2024
Reasoning models — OpenAI o1 “thinks” before answering — compute spent at answer time, not just training
2025
MoE + distillation + open weights — DeepSeek R1: frontier ability gets radically cheaper; big models teach small ones
2026
Agentic harnesses — Claude Code · Cowork-class agents bring delegation to general office work
The speed of adoption
Months to reach 100 million users — shorter bar = faster
ChatGPT
2 mo
TikTok
~9 mo
Instagram
~30 mo
Fastest consumer ramp on record (UBS/Reuters, 2023).
The methods on the left are the vocabulary for the whole course — each returns on a later slide.

ARCHIVED SOURCE NOTES
HOW TO PRESENT —
1) Walk the timeline TOP TO BOTTOM, metronome pace — say the METHOD name in bold each time.
2) Slow down twice: 2022 (RLHF) and 2024 (models that think before answering).
3) On 2017, tell the title story: “Attention Is All You Need” — ATTENTION is the mechanism that lets the model weigh which earlier words matter most when predicting the next one; the paper’s bold claim was that attention ALONE suffices — the older machinery could be dropped. (The title is widely described as a playful nod to “All You Need Is Love.”)
4) Right card: ChatGPT reached 100M users in two months; TikTok ~nine; Instagram ~two and a half years.

TRY IT (optional, spoken — not one of the seven numbered exercises) —
TYPE THIS → “Explain the 2017 AI paper ‘Attention Is All You Need’ like I’m new to AI: what is attention, why did the title claim it’s ALL you need, and what did it replace? Under 120 words.”
WHY → the definition lands in their course log, accurately, from their own tool.

ACRONYMS —
GPT = Generative Pre-trained Transformer. RLHF = Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback.
MoE = Mixture of Experts (defined properly in Part 2). o1 = OpenAI’s first reasoning model. R1 = DeepSeek’s open reasoning model.

CONTENT —
A multi-company user-growth line is NOT buildable honestly (metrics differ: weekly vs monthly actives vs downloads) — the time-to-100M chart is the one honest shape (single source).
Kept for questions: 88% of organizations use AI somewhere (Stanford AI Index 2026), but agent deployment is still single-digit % — everyone chats, almost nobody delegates. That gap is this course.
Vendor adoption numbers are marketing until independently reproduced.

title: The hardware behind model development
notes:
MODE: REFERENCE

TIME: 0:10

PURPOSE: Preserve depth for self-study without consuming live practice time.

LAND THIS: Scale, data, and computing made modern systems practical.

SAY:
- Computing, data, and model design jointly supported progress.
- The hardware details are reference material, not today’s learning target.

DO: None.

BRIDGE: Move to “How a language model produces an answer”.

IF LATE: SKIP

SOURCE DETAIL FOR SELF-STUDY
PART 1 · A SHORT HISTORY
6
WHY AI HAPPENED NOW
The hardware story — chips, Nvidia, data centers
① A 60-year tailwind
Moore’s law (1965): chips double their transistors every ~2 years.
1971: 2,300 → 2024: 208 billion
2026 status: slowing to ~3-year doublings — not dead, no longer enough alone.
② The accident
Gaming chips WERE AI chips: both need millions of tiny calculations at once.
2006 — Nvidia’s CUDA lets anyone program a graphics card.
2012 — AlexNet: two consumer gaming cards, six days, beats 30 years of hand-built AI.
③ Moore’s pace vs AI’s appetite
Y axis: training compute per model, in FLOP (one FLOP = one arithmetic operation) — log scale
10¹⁸
10²¹
10²⁴
AlexNet
GPT-2
GPT-3
GPT-4 (est.)
Moore’s pace
2012
2023
At Moore’s pace since 2012: ×45.  Actual: ×45,000,000.
GPT-4 ≈ 2×10²⁵ FLOP: ~200,000 years on AlexNet’s two cards — a ~25,000-GPU data-center hall: ~3 months.
④ Why the data centers
TRAIN — One frontier model: 16,000+ GPUs running for months (Llama 3.1, 2024).
SERVE — Then a billion people use it — around the clock, every day.
POWER — One large AI data center ≈ the electricity of 100,000 homes; the biggest under construction ≈ 2 million (IEA).
~$700B of build-out planned for 2026 — much announced, not yet built.
The shovel-seller: Nvidia — first reached $1T May 2023 · $4T Jul 2025 · $5T Oct 2025 · ~$5.6T today: the world’s most valuable company, and 92% of its revenue is now AI data centers.

ARCHIVED SOURCE NOTES
HOW TO PRESENT —
1) Frame: “software got the headlines — hardware made it possible. Four beats, left to right.”
2) ① Moore’s law in one sentence: chips doubled their transistors every ~2 years for 50 years — 1971: 2,300; 2024: 208 billion, ~90 million times more. Status 2026: slowing to ~3-year doublings, not dead.
3) ② The accident story, told plainly: in 2012 three university researchers couldn’t afford a supercomputer, so they trained their network on TWO consumer gaming cards. Six days later it beat 30 years of hand-built AI. Every AI company today is still scaling up that trick. (CUDA, 2006, is why it was even possible — Nvidia had let anyone program a graphics card, and had a five-year head start when AI came calling.)
4) ③ The chart — the punchline of the slide: if AI compute had grown at Moore’s pace since 2012 it would be ~45× bigger. It is ~45 MILLION times bigger. The gap was bought with chips, clusters, and electricity — that gap IS the data-center boom.
5) ④ Train / serve / power — and the honest caveat aloud: a lot of what you read about is ANNOUNCED, not built.
6) Amber band — the shovel-seller: the most valuable company on Earth makes no chatbot, no phone, no search engine. It sells the shovels. Ten years ago it was “the video-game graphics company.” (This tees up Part 2: when one cheap Chinese model made investors doubt how many shovels are needed, Nvidia lost $589B in a day.)

BRIDGE —
“That’s the machinery. Now — what is the model itself actually doing? Under the hood.”

ACRONYMS —
GPU = Graphics Processing Unit — thousands of simple cores doing the same math at once (a CPU: a few smart cores, one task at a time).
CUDA = Nvidia’s software for running ANY computation on its graphics chips (2006) — the moat is the software, not just the chips.
IEA = International Energy Agency. FLOP = floating-point operation (the compute unit behind the chart).

CONTENT —
v1.7 new slide (owner request: Moore’s law, Nvidia’s role, chips⇄AI, why data centers — intro level). Every fact sourced in notes/research/r22_hardware_story.md: Moore 1965/1975 · Intel-CEO 3-year cadence · Blackwell 208B transistors (Mar 2024) · CUDA 2006 · AlexNet two GTX 580s (NeurIPS 2012 paper) · chart = Epoch AI database (GPT-4 point is an ESTIMATE — labeled) · Llama 3.1 16,000+ H100s (Meta, Jul 2024) · IEA Apr 2025 (415 TWh 2024 → ~945 TWh 2030; 100K-homes comparison) · capex ~$700B+ 2026 (CNBC Feb 2026, analyst tallies vary) · Nvidia milestones $1T–$5T with dates + ~$5.56T and 92% data-center revenue (Q2 FY2027, Aug 2026).
If asked about “Huang’s law” (AI chips beating Moore’s law): Nvidia’s claim for whole SYSTEMS; independent measurement (Epoch) puts GPU price-performance doubling at ~2.5 years — say “the marketing outruns the measurement.”
Stargate, if asked: announced Jan 2025 at “up to $500B”; by mid-2026 ~7 GW PLANNED across 7 US sites, first campus (Abilene, TX) partially live — announced ≠ built.
US–China chip angle, one line if asked: US export restrictions since Oct 2022; an Apr 2025 license rule forced Nvidia to write down $5.5B on its China-market chip.
v1.12 Y-AXIS, made explicit (owner request): the axis is TRAINING COMPUTE in FLOP — floating-point operations, one FLOP = one arithmetic operation (a single multiply or add) — on a log scale from 10^17 to 10^26; ticks at 10^18 / 10^21 / 10^24. Say it as one variable: “everything on this chart is counted in the same unit — how many little arithmetic operations it took to train the model.” The data-center equivalence under the chart: GPT-4 ≈ 2.1×10^25 FLOP (Epoch estimate). On AlexNet’s two GTX 580s (~3.2×10^12 FLOP/s combined, perfect efficiency) that is ~2×10^5 years — the “~200,000 years” line, an arithmetic illustration, not a measured fact. The “~25,000-GPU hall, ~3 months” figure is the widely reported industry estimate for GPT-4’s training cluster (SemiAnalysis-derived; vendor-unconfirmed — say “reported estimate” if pressed). One more anchor if useful: Llama 3.1 on the TRAIN tile used 16,000+ GPUs — that IS a data-center hall; the chart is why those halls exist.
6

PART 1 · HOW LLMS WORK
7
UNDER THE HOOD
A prediction engine, sent to finishing school
1 · Pretraining
Months, trillions of words: learn to predict the next token on internet-scale text. Language, facts, and reasoning patterns compress into billions of learned weights.
2 · Instruction tuning
Curated example dialogues teach it to follow instructions and answer questions — instead of just continuing your text.
3 · Human feedback (RLHF)
People rank outputs; the model is tuned toward helpful, honest, harmless. And it never stops: your thumbs-up today is preference data for the NEXT model.
Knowledge is frozen at the cutoff — with escape hatches. 
Training ends months before release. Many assistants compensate: live web search pulls today’s pages into the prompt; RAG (concept 3) plugs in your own documents.
Why prompting exists: 
the model completes your text — the prompt is the only steering wheel you have. A complete prompt doesn’t make the model smarter: it deletes wrong guesses.
PROMPT 2/7
Narrowing the guesses — two separate sends
STEP 1 · TYPE THIS → “Finish this sentence 5 different ways: We should move the launch date because”
WHY → no facts yet — watch it scatter across guesses.
STEP 2 · TYPE THIS → “Now 5 more ways, knowing: B2B software firm, competitor launches May 3, our beta ends April 20.”
WHY → your facts didn’t make it smarter — they deleted wrong guesses.
✂ copy-paste, don’t retype: tab EX2-Guesses of your Course Workbook

1) Title metaphor first: “a prediction engine, sent to finishing school.”
2) Three cards LEFT TO RIGHT — pretraining, instruction tuning, human feedback. On card 3, land the after-ship line: RLHF never really stops — every thumbs-up/down you click, and on personal accounts your chats themselves, become the preference data that trains the next model. (That is exactly what “trains on your data by default” means on the trust slide in Part 2.)
3) LEFT callout: the cutoff — AND its two escape hatches: live web search, and RAG for your own documents.
4) RIGHT callout, slowly — the thesis of the course: the prompt is the only steering wheel; a complete prompt DELETES WRONG GUESSES.

Send 1 scatters: budget, staffing, quality. Send 2 orbits May 3 and April 20.
Debrief line: “Grade the directions, not the sentences.”

BRIDGE —
“Six concepts, quick — starting with what the model actually reads.”

RAG = Retrieval-Augmented Generation — concept 3, shortly.

title: Tokens and practical limits
notes:
MODE: REFERENCE

TIME: 0:10

PURPOSE: Preserve depth for self-study without consuming live practice time.

LAND THIS: Tokens affect context, cost, and instruction clarity.

SAY:
- Tokens are units a model processes, not a fixed number of words.
- The useful consequence is that context and output have practical limits.

DO: None.

BRIDGE: Move to “Context, saved history, and memory”.

IF LATE: SKIP

SOURCE DETAIL FOR SELF-STUDY
PART 1 · CORE CONCEPTS
8
CONCEPT 1 · TOKENS
The model reads bricks, not letters
Text is chopped into tokens — word chunks from a fixed vocabulary. Common words are one token; rare ones get built from pieces (“ham·bur·ger”).
Rules of thumb (English): 1 token ≈ 4 characters ≈ ¾ of a word. A 50-page document ≈ 25–35K tokens.
The model never sees letters — “strawberry” arrives as one or two IDs. The famous letter-counting fails of 2024 are patched now; what still breaks: exact word counts and “count your own tokens” (every tier), character-precise edits (free/fast tiers).
Everything is priced and limited in tokens — input and output. Output tokens cost ~5× input, because generation is serial.
LEGO bricks of text
Common words are pre-molded bricks; rare words get built from pieces. You pay by the brick.
Analyzing
the
supplier

first

pass
yield
So what, for daily work: 
paste-heavy prompts burn budget and context fast · non-English and dense technical text cost more tokens · use AI for language, software for characters (counts, checksums, exact IDs).
PROMPT 3/7
Bricks, not letters
TYPE THIS → “Explain AI tokens to a high-school student in under 80 words: use a LEGO-brick analogy, show one word splitting into tokens, and end with why tokens set my AI’s cost and limits.”
WHY → the definition lands in your course log — the analogy the best explainers use.
✂ copy-paste, don’t retype: tab EX3-Tokens of your Course Workbook

ARCHIVED SOURCE NOTES
HOW TO PRESENT —
1) Title first: “the model reads bricks, not letters.”
2) Left bullets; STOP on the bold third and tell the story ARC: 2024 — models famously miscounted the r’s in “strawberry” and the internet laughed; 2025 — vendors patched it (partly memorization: days after GPT-5 launched, its FAST path insisted “blueberry” has three b’s while its thinking path got it right); 2026 — the lesson that never changed: it reads bricks, not letters. NEVER run strawberry or blueberry live — both are famous now.
3) Right card: the brick strip — “this is exactly how your sentence arrives: eight bricks, eight numbers.”
4) THE live demo (safe — it shows the bricks, it can’t “get it right”): open platform.openai.com/tokenizer (PRELOAD it; backup: tiktokenizer.vercel.app) and paste attendees’ NAMES and company jargon — common words stay whole, rare words shatter into colored chunks.
5) Near-safe live model variant if the room wants proof from the AI itself: ask “how many tokens is this paragraph?” then show the real count on the tokenizer page — models cannot count their own tokens, on ANY tier, and the reveal is exactly the lesson.
6) Teal card: the three daily-work consequences.

TRY IT — PROMPT 3/7 (copy from tab EX3-Tokens)
One send; the AI teaches the concept into their log.
Recovery (answers differ across the room): “every vendor has its own brick set — the bricks are always there, the letters never are.”

BRIDGE —
“If text is bricks — how many bricks fit on the desk?”

ACRONYMS —
ID = identifier — to the model each token is just a number. K = thousand.

CONTENT —
v1.7: capability claim re-verified 2026-09-10 (r23_tokens_grok_hallucination.md, owner challenge): strawberry-class counting is fixed on current frontier models (partly memorized — the Aug-2025 blueberry incident); still failing with evidence: character-position edits ~33–44% accuracy on non-reasoning tiers (CharBench 2025/26) · paragraph-scale letter counts on fast tiers · exact word counts on ALL tiers · counting own tokens on ALL tiers (arXiv:2502.06258). Reasoning modes pass letter tasks by spelling out — a paid, token-burning workaround, not letter-vision. Re-verify at every refresh; this claim ages fast.
v1.6: prompt finalized from the explainer research (r17) — LEGO validated as the dominant popular analogy; tokenizer-page demo recommended over any word trick.
Token math preview: tokens also explain context windows (next slide) and the bill (later this part).
ART — the LEGO wall + robot hand at the top of the right card is an owner-generated illustration (R16).

title: Context, saved history, and memory
notes:
MODE: TEACH

TIME: 0:50

PURPOSE: Build a concept required for the next application.

LAND THIS: Saved history, active context, and cross-chat memory are different things.

SAY:
- Use the desk analogy only for active context.
- Closing a window does not necessarily delete a saved conversation.
- A long chat may omit or compress earlier material. Carry important requirements in a short handoff.

DO: None.

BRIDGE: Move to “Answers grounded in documents”.

IF LATE: COMPRESS

SOURCE DETAIL FOR SELF-STUDY
PART 1 · CORE CONCEPTS
9
CONCEPT 2 · CONTEXT WINDOW
A desk, not a filing cabinet
The context window is working memory for one conversation: your question, the system prompt, chat history, attached files, and search results must all fit on the desk.
Close the chat and the desk is swept clean. Nothing persists unless a memory feature or a saved file re-loads it.
By 2026, ~1M tokens (≈750,000 words) is the flagship standard. Consumer apps often enforce smaller limits than the raw model.
In very long chats the middle gets skimmed — accuracy is highest at the start and the end (“lost in the middle”).
What’s on the desk right now
System prompt & instructions
Every prior turn — both sides
Attached documents
Tool & search results
Habits that exploit the desk: 
① long documents at the TOP, question at the END (up to ~30% better answers) · ② label multiple documents · ③ new topic → new chat · ④ long thread → run the handoff move below.
A desk with a filing cabinet? Persistent files, notes and standing instructions are what agentic tools bolt onto the desk — Part 5. Pros call this CONTEXT ENGINEERING: the prompt is the briefing; context is everything on the desk — even what nobody typed.
PROMPT 4/7
The desk — explained, then carried
STEP 1 · TYPE THIS → “Explain your context window like I’m a 5th grader: the desk, what fits on it, and what happens when I close this chat. Under 100 words.”
WHY → the AI describes its own working memory, plainly.
STEP 2 · TYPE THIS → (homework) “Summarize our chat so far in under 80 words, titled HANDOFF.”
WHY → tonight, paste into a fresh chat, ask “where was I?” — it picks up your course.
✂ copy-paste, don’t retype: tab EX4-Handoff of your Course Workbook

HOW TO PRESENT —
1) The analogy first: “a desk, not a filing cabinet.”
2) Left bullets; on the bold one, draw the U-shape in the air — attention high at the start, sags in the middle, high at the end.
3) Right card: the four things on the desk right now.
4) Teal card: the four habits — habit ④ is about to be performed.
5) Amber card: one sentence — the filing-cabinet teaser for Part 5. Plant the seed, move on.

TRY IT — PROMPT 4/7 (copy from tab EX4-Handoff)
Step 1 in class; step 2 is homework in the same thread.
Recovery (someone’s fresh chat knows unpasted things): “your tool has a filing cabinet bolted to the desk — hold that thought for Part 5.”

BRIDGE —
“And what if what you need was never on the desk? RAG.”

ACRONYMS —
1M = one million tokens.

CONTENT —
“Lost in the middle” = Liu et al. 2023 (TACL). The up-to-~30% figure is Anthropic’s own long-context guidance.
1M-token flagship standard verified Aug 2026 across Claude, GPT-5.x, Gemini, and the Chinese open-weight flagships.

title: Answers grounded in documents
notes:
MODE: TEACH

TIME: 0:50

PURPOSE: Build a concept required for the next application.

LAND THIS: Retrieval can ground an answer in documents, but the source and citation still need checking.

SAY:
- Introduce retrieval-augmented generation as looking up relevant passages before answering.
- An outdated agreement can support a well-cited but wrong answer for today’s decision.
- Retention, training use, and access controls depend on the actual service and configuration.

DO: None.

BRIDGE: Move to “Instructions, sources, and model adaptation”.

IF LATE: COMPRESS

SOURCE DETAIL FOR SELF-STUDY
PART 1 · CORE CONCEPTS
10
CONCEPT 3 · RAG
An open-book exam — audit the librarian
The problem RAG solves: the model’s knowledge is frozen and public; your work runs on private documents it has never seen — and must never be trained on.
1 · Ask
Plain question: “What does the supplier agreement say about re-inspection?”
2 · Retrieve
Semantic search finds the most relevant passages — by meaning, not keywords.
3 · Augment
Those passages are placed on the model’s desk, behind the scenes.
4 · Generate
The model answers from the supplied text — and cites where it looked.
Why enterprises build on it: 
current (re-index in minutes, no retraining) · checkable (citations to the exact passage) · private (retrieval feeds one answer, teaches the model nothing) · access-aware.
The failure mode to respect: 
fetch the wrong page — an outdated revision, a near-miss document — and the model still writes a fluent, confident, CITED answer from it. Check the citation, not just the prose.
You already use this. Our internal company assistant — the one where you upload documentation and “talk” to it — is RAG in production. Every step on this slide happens each time you ask it a question.

ARCHIVED SOURCE NOTES
HOW TO PRESENT —
1) Expand the acronym ONCE, then the analogy: an open-book exam — a librarian fetches pages from YOUR documents; the student writes from those pages.
2) Four step cards LEFT TO RIGHT.
3) Green card: current, checkable, private, access-aware.
4) Red card, slowly: wrong page → fluent, confident, CITED, wrong. “Check the citation, not the prose.”
5) Teal band: “you’ve been running this loop all along” — keep it generic, no product names.

BRIDGE —
“When do you prompt, when do you retrieve, when do you fine-tune? The escalation ladder.”

ACRONYMS —
RAG = Retrieval-Augmented Generation.

CONTENT —
Retrieval ≠ training is the privacy point to repeat.
This is the engine behind internal document assistants and Copilot-over-SharePoint.
ART — the open-book-exam scene (robot writing from the book, librarian delivering a glowing page) is an owner-generated illustration (R16); gesture at it when you say the analogy.
